text: Habba Khatoon (Kashmiri: [habɨ xoːt̪uːn]; born Zoon Rather or Zuni, Kashmiri: زوٗن, lit. 'Moon'), also known as The Nightingale of Kashmir, was a 16th-century Kashmiri Muslim poet and ascetic. She was the consort of King Yousuf Shah Chak, though scholarly debate exists over whether she was a lower-status mistress or a member of his harem. Born in the village of Chandur (Kashmiri: Tsandhor) in Pampore, Pulwama district, her birth name was Zoon, given to her due to her beauty. Her father, Abdi Rathar of Chandhur, was a well-to-do and courageous farmer who arranged for her education with a village maulvi, teaching her the Quran and Persian classics, which were popular at the time. She learned works like Gulistan and Bostan and gained recognition beyond her village. Her parents intended to marry her to a peasant boy, Aziz Lone, who was uninterested in her charm and love, leading her to endure hardship—fetching water, gathering firewood, spinning, and enduring criticism from her mother-in-law and society. In her song "Tche Kyoho Vaatiyo Myaeni Marnai" (What do you stand to gain by my death?), she reflects on her suffering and questions the value of her death, concluding with introspection. Seeking solace, she consulted Khwaja Masud, who gave her consolation and reportedly coined the name Habba Khatoon, which she adopted. One of her famous songs, "Wolo Myaeni Poshey Madano" (Come, my flowery Cupid), expresses her longing and bitterness. According to legend, Yousuf Shah Chak, the last independent emperor of Kashmir, heard her singing under a chinar tree and fell in love, leading to her entry into the palace around 1570. She became a central figure in his life, and the couple visited natural sites like Gulmarg, Aharabal, Achabal, and Sonamarg, with a hillock in Gurez named after her. During this time, Kashmir faced political instability, with the Chak dynasty weakened and the Mughal emperor Akbar eyeing the region. Yousuf Shah Chak lost the throne in 1580 and was later supported by Akbar, who helped him regain it in 1581 through Raja Man Singh’s intervention. After Yousuf’s departure, Habba Khatoon remained in Kashmir for nearly twenty years, moving without attachments. She composed songs like "Harmukh Bartal," expressing her sorrow and longing for her husband. Though Persian words like 'shamaa,' 'ishq,' and 'burqa' were already in Kashmiri, she used them sparingly, preserving the authenticity and musicality of her native language. She developed a new musical form, Raasti-Kashmiri, modeled on Raasti-Farsi, and mastered the Persian raga Muqaami-Iran. Her poems, including Harmukh Bartal, Char kar myon maalinyo, and Vaervain saeth vaar chas no, are known as Yadhaaq in Kashmiri. The taqleqkar of loal poetry was praised by Kalhana in Rajtarangini. The hillock in Gurez Valley and an underpass in Mughalpura, Lahore, are named after her, and the Indian Coast Guard named a ship CGS Habba Khatoon in her honor.

Habba Khatoon was skilled in both poetic and musical styles, and naturally made her own contribution through a new composition called Raasti-Kashmiri, which is based on Raasti-Farsi and is sung during the last quarter of the night. She gained recognition for her expertise in the Persian raga Muqaami-Iran. Her poems, including Harmukh Bartal, Char kar myon maalinyo, Vaervain saeth vaar chas no, and others, are known as Yadhaaq in the Kashmiri language. The pioneer of loal poetry, referred to as the taqleqkar, was lauded by Kalhana in his work Rajtarangini, who described the poet’s insight as surpassing the stream of ambrosia, resulting in a lasting embodiment of glory for both the poet and others. A hillock in the Gurez Valley, Kashmir, is named after her, and an underpass in Mughalpura, Lahore, bears her name. Additionally, the Indian Coast Guard named a ship, CGS Habba Khatoon, in her honor.
